title: Fast Radio Bursts Follow Star Formation Almost Instantly
hook: Mysterious millisecond flashes from across the universe closely track where new stars are being born — with almost no time lag, ruling out one of the leading theories of what causes them.
key_points: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-long flashes of radio waves from distant galaxies; what triggers most of them has been debated for years.
A new statistical analysis of the CHIME/FRB catalog found the FRB rate peaks at the same cosmic epoch as star formation, with a delay of only 0.1-0.3 billion years.
That's too short to fit the multi-billion-year delay expected if most FRBs come from old compact-binary mergers (like colliding neutron stars).
The result instead favors young stellar remnants — most likely magnetars born in core-collapse supernovae — as the dominant source.
content_html: For years, one open question about fast radio bursts (FRBs) — brief, powerful flashes of radio waves from far outside our galaxy — has been what actually triggers them. Two broad pictures competed: young magnetars, the intensely magnetic remnants left behind almost immediately after a massive star explodes as a supernova, or old compact-object mergers, like colliding neutron stars, which typically take billions of years to happen after their parent stars were born.
extra_html: Astronomers Yi-Ying Wang, Yin-Jie Li, and Yi-Zhong Fan tackled the question with a hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the CHIME/FRB catalog, jointly modeling the observed bursts, their brightness, and the redshifts of their host galaxies while correcting for what the survey could and couldn't detect. Across a range of models, the reconstructed FRB rate peaked at the same cosmic epoch as the universe's star-formation history, with a mean delay of just 0.1 to 0.3 billion years — consistent with essentially no delay at all. That's far too short for the multi-billion-year lag expected from compact-binary mergers, ruling out mergers as the dominant channel and instead pointing to progenitors tied to young stellar remnants, most notably magnetars forged in core-collapse supernovae.

flashcards.prompt: What did the new analysis of the CHIME/FRB catalog find about the timing of FRBs relative to star formation?

choices.text: FRBs track star formation almost instantly, with only a 0.1-0.3 billion-year delay
FRBs lag star formation by many billions of years
FRBs show no relationship to star formation at all

flashcards.explanation_html: The FRB rate peaks at the same cosmic epoch as star formation with only a short delay — far too brief for an old-population origin.

flashcards.prompt: Why does this short delay rule out compact-binary mergers as the dominant FRB source?
flashcards.back_html: Mergers of old compact objects like neutron stars take billions of years to occur after their stars form. A near-instant delay instead points to young remnants — most likely magnetars from core-collapse supernovae.
